title: Build the identity foundation
subtitle: Windows Server 2025 · Active Directory and DNS
scope: Two new Windows Server 2025 Desktop Experience virtual machines on an isolated network. Sample values below must be reconciled with the final recording. Procedures are documentation-based and have not been executed against your environment.

sources.title: Microsoft · Install Active Directory Domain Services
NIST · Risk Management Framework SP 800-37 Rev. 2

chapters.title: Give every system a purpose
chapters.outcome: Record the starting configuration and explain what the two controllers will do.
chapters.intro: Start by understanding the services you are about to build. Then record the names, addresses, and dependencies for two controllers in the same domain.
steps: Prepare two separate VMs

Use new, patched Windows Server 2025 Desktop Experience installations with console access and the required administrative credentials. Keep the virtual network isolated. Obtain approved media and updates through your established offline process.
Record names and addresses

Rename the servers SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 and restart as needed. Use 10.0.10.10/24 and 10.0.10.11/24 for this sample. No gateway is needed for this same-subnet exercise; the wider network requires its own approved routing plan.
Set the DNS starting point

For the first DC that will host DNS, use its own static address, 10.0.10.10. Point DC02 at DC01 before promotion. Verify clocks are aligned and document the intended internal time source. Do not add an internet resolver or external forwarder to this isolated network.
chapters.expected: The two names and static addresses match your plan. DC02 points to 10.0.10.10 for DNS. Record actual time-source output; a configured address alone does not prove time synchronization.
chapters.mistake: A DNS server address configured on a network adapter does not install DNS. DC01 will not answer DNS queries until its DNS service is installed and running.
chapters.network: Both controllers are planned. The platform and network exist, but domain services have not been built yet.

control.name: Baseline Configuration
control.body: Start with a record of the intended components and settings. As the build changes, keep that record aligned with what actually exists.
control.question: Which values are design decisions, and which observations show the actual starting state?
control.evidence: A dated build sheet containing hostnames, addresses, OS builds, and the chosen domain name.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record your VM names, OS builds, addresses, DNS settings, and any differences from the sample.
checklist: I recorded the two distinct hostnames and static addresses.
I confirmed the isolated network and DNS starting point.
I documented the time source and remaining prerequisites.

quiz.prompt: Before promoting DC02, where should it look for the existing domain's DNS?
answers: DC01, once its domain DNS is available
Only itself, before DNS is installed
quiz.feedback: DC02 needs to locate the existing directory through DNS. In this sample, DC01 provides that service first.

chapters.title: Create the first domain controller
chapters.outcome: Create the sample forest and bring AD DS and DNS online on DC01.
chapters.intro: A new forest establishes the directory's initial boundary. Here, sbd.test is a sample domain, not an existing company domain. Follow this path only for a new forest.
steps: Add the server role
On DC01, open Server Manager → Manage → Add Roles and Features. Choose the local server and Active Directory Domain Services, including its management tools.
Create the forest

Select Promote this server to a domain controller, then Add a new forest. Enter sbd.test. For this all-2025 sample, select Windows Server 2025 functional levels. Include DNS and the global catalog. Enter and confirm a unique Directory Services Restore Mode password on the server.
Review and promote

Review DNS options, the SBD NetBIOS name, paths, and prerequisite results. A parent-zone delegation is not required for this isolated .test forest. Resolve blocking errors, install, and allow the restart. Then inspect the services and domain.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName
Get-Service NTDS,DNS,Netlogon
Get-SmbShare -Name SYSVOL,NETLOGON
chapters.expected: The domain is sbd.test with NetBIOS name SBD. NTDS, DNS, and Netlogon are running, and SYSVOL and NETLOGON shares exist. Investigate missing services or shares before moving on.
chapters.mistake: Installing the AD DS role is only the first part. The promotion wizard creates the domain controller; a completed role installation alone is not a completed forest.
chapters.network: DC01 now provides AD DS and DNS. DC02 is still planned; no replication relationship is shown yet.

control.name: Configuration Settings
control.body: Record the settings you selected and why. An installation result is useful evidence, but a defensible configuration record also identifies the applicable requirement and any approved exception.
control.question: Why were these domain, DNS, and functional-level settings chosen?
control.evidence: Promotion settings, prerequisite results, and post-restart domain and service checks. Keep recovery passwords out of the evidence.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record the domain, promotion outcome, service checks, and the file names of your screenshots or saved output. Do not enter passwords.
checklist: I checked the domain name after restart.
I verified NTDS, DNS, Netlogon, SYSVOL, and NETLOGON.
I documented configuration choices without recording credentials.

quiz.prompt: What turns an AD DS role installation into a domain controller?
quiz.feedback: Promotion configures the directory role for a new forest or an existing domain. Merely adding the role is insufficient.

chapters.title: Give the domain a second service point
chapters.outcome: Promote DC02 into the existing domain and inspect the replication relationship.
chapters.intro: A second domain controller gives the domain another live service point. Read why this is a standard availability practice, then add DC02 and verify the result.
steps: Reach the existing directory
On DC02, confirm DNS points to 10.0.10.10. Query the domain service records and resolve SBD-DC01.sbd.test. Check network reachability and clock alignment before promotion.
Add a controller to this domain

Install the AD DS role and management tools. In the promotion wizard choose Add a domain controller to an existing domain, enter sbd.test, and authenticate with an authorized Domain Admin account. Select DNS and global catalog, leave Read only domain controller unselected, and set the DSRM password securely.
Finish and inspect

Review site placement, replication source, and prerequisite results; install and restart. Keep DC02 using DC01 for DNS until initial inbound replication is healthy. Then document the final internal resolver order for both DCs, retaining a reachable partner and self as appropriate to the design.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * |
  Select-Object HostName, IPv4Address, IsGlobalCatalog
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl SBD-DC02
chapters.expected: Both hostnames appear with the intended addresses and global catalog roles. After initial convergence, replication checks show successful recent attempts and no unresolved replication failures. Inspect errors rather than assuming the restart completed replication.
chapters.mistake: Choosing Add a new forest creates a different directory. For this chapter, DC02 joins the domain established by DC01.
chapters.network: Both controllers provide AD DS and DNS. The animated relationship represents directory replication, not a measured packet capture.

control.name: System Backup
control.body: Use the second controller to discuss the difference between service availability and recoverability. Replication carries current changes, including damaging ones. Protected backups and a tested recovery process remain separate requirements.
control.question: What would happen if an unwanted directory change replicated to both controllers?
control.evidence: Replication results plus a separate record of the backup and recovery requirements still to implement and test.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Record both controllers, replication status and collection time, plus any failures or follow-up actions.
checklist: I confirmed DC02 belongs to the same domain.
I inspected recent replication attempts and unresolved errors.
I can explain why replication does not replace a backup.

quiz.prompt: A damaging directory change reaches both controllers. What does that illustrate?
answers: Replication and historical recovery are different capabilities
quiz.feedback: Both controllers can hold the same unwanted change. Recovery requires protected backups and an appropriate, tested recovery procedure.

chapters.title: Ask the services to prove they work
chapters.outcome: Query each DNS service explicitly and inspect domain-controller health.
chapters.intro: A service can be running while its configuration is wrong. Query each DNS server by address so the result tells you which server answered. Capture actual results and failures in your evidence record.
steps: Query each DNS service

Run the checks below in an administrative Windows PowerShell session with the server tools available. Query the domain controller locator SRV records separately on DC01 and DC02. SRV means service record.
Check the host records

Resolve SBD-DC01.sbd.test and SBD-DC02.sbd.test against both DNS servers. Expect 10.0.10.10 and 10.0.10.11 respectively. A locator response does not, by itself, prove that every listed host is reachable.
Review health in context

Run DCDiag and review each result. In an isolated environment, classify any external-resolution failures against the intended design. The workstation in this scene is a test viewpoint; joining and validating a real Windows client is an optional extension after routing and client prerequisites are ready.
chapters.command:
$servers = '10.0.10.10','10.0.10.11'
foreach ($server in $servers) {
  Write-Output "DNS server: $server"
  Resolve-DnsName '_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.sbd.test' -Type SRV -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC01.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
  Resolve-DnsName 'SBD-DC02.sbd.test' -Type A -Server $server
}
dcdiag /test:DNS /e /v
repadmin /replsummary
chapters.expected: Each DNS service returns domain locator records for the configured controllers and the correct host addresses. Review DCDiag findings and replication failures individually. Save output with host, time, and interpretation; do not record an automatic pass because the command ran.
chapters.mistake: A successful ping confirms limited IP reachability, not DNS service discovery, directory replication, or authentication.
chapters.network: Follow a DNS query from the test viewpoint to either DC. Switch the resolver to see the alternative service path. The core represents the routing dependency when a client is on another VLAN.

control.name: Identification and Authentication
control.body: DNS is a dependency that helps users locate identity services. DNS test output supports understanding that dependency; it does not demonstrate all authentication requirements, such as multifactor authentication or account policy.
control.question: What do these checks establish, and what authentication behavior still needs its own test?
control.evidence: Separate query results for each resolver, health-test output, and a short statement of what was and was not tested.

chapters.evidencePrompt: For each DNS server, record the observed SRV and A-record results, test time, failures, and what the results establish.
checklist: I queried DC01 and DC02 separately.
I compared returned names and addresses with the plan.
I reviewed errors and recorded the limits of these checks.

quiz.prompt: What does a successful DNS locator query establish?
answers: The queried server returned the requested service records
The system is authorized to operate
quiz.feedback: The query demonstrates a particular DNS response. Reachability, authentication, control effectiveness, and authorization require additional evidence and decisions.

chapters.title: Leave a build someone else can understand
chapters.outcome: Assemble your configuration record, test evidence, and remaining work.
chapters.intro: The useful deliverable is a build you can explain and check again. Your evidence record connects each action with an observed result and identifies what remains unresolved.
steps: Describe the final state
Record the domain, both controllers, DNS resolver choices, site placement, and actual role holders. Preserve the distinction between the intended design and observed configuration.
Keep a small evidence set

Store your environment outputs locally with descriptive filenames and collection times. In this companion, write a short summary and the file references; the form does not upload or collect your screenshots, server output, or credentials.
Plan the next check

List remaining hardening, auditing, backup, recovery, and client-validation work. Assign an owner or next action. Revisit checks after relevant configuration changes. Export the evidence record before moving devices.
chapters.command:
Get-ADDomain |
  Select-Object DNSRoot, PDCEmulator, RIDMaster, InfrastructureMaster
Get-ADForest |
  Select-Object RootDomain, SchemaMaster, DomainNamingMaster
chapters.expected: The record identifies the actual role holders and links configuration decisions to dated test results. Open issues remain visible. Lesson completion records learning activity; it is not a system authorization decision.
chapters.mistake: A diagram becoming complete does not establish that your VM passed a check. The model tells the lesson story; your observations establish what happened in your environment.
chapters.network: The identity foundation is complete for this course. Continue into the full network to see the services that later lessons can add.

control.name: Maintain the configuration and its evidence
control.body: Risk Management Framework (RMF) assessment evaluates selected controls using evidence. Monitoring revisits the security state as the system changes. These learning examples must be tailored to the applicable requirements; selected control labels do not establish compliance or authorization.
control.question: What change would make you rerun a DNS or replication check?
control.evidence: The build record, dated verification output, unresolved issues, and the next review trigger.

chapters.evidencePrompt: Summarize the final state, reference your evidence files, and list remaining work with a next action or review trigger.
checklist: I linked configuration choices to dated observations.
I recorded unresolved issues and the next review trigger.
I exported my evidence record for safekeeping.

quiz.prompt: Which event is a useful reason to revisit the evidence?
answers: Only the anniversary of the video
A relevant configuration change or new finding
quiz.feedback: Changes and findings can affect prior conclusions. A monitoring plan defines when and how to reassess the relevant security state.

foundations.title: What is Active Directory?
foundations.summary: The shared directory behind domain identities.
blocks: A directory for people and computers

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the Windows Server directory service. It stores objects such as user accounts, computer accounts, and groups, together with their attributes. Administrators use this shared directory to organize identities and manage access consistently.
The domain and the controller

A domain is a logical collection of directory objects, named here sbd.test. A domain controller (DC) is a server running AD DS that stores and serves that directory. DC01 and DC02 are two servers serving the same domain. A forest contains one or more domains; this build starts with one.
Identity, permissions, and policy

Authentication checks who is signing in. Authorization determines what that identity may access. Signing in successfully does not grant access to every resource: the destination service still applies its permissions. Groups make it practical to assign access to roles instead of managing every person separately.
Organization and consistent settings

Organizational units (OUs) organize objects and support delegated administration and Group Policy. Group Policy applies centrally managed settings to users and computers. A global catalog helps find directory objects across a forest; both controllers in this course provide that role.
foundations.takeaway: AD DS provides directory and identity services. DNS helps clients find those services. Each has a distinct job.
foundations.prompt: Explain the difference between the sbd.test domain and the SBD-DC01 server.

foundations.title: What is DNS?
foundations.summary: The name and service directory that makes AD discoverable.
blocks: Names become reachable addresses

Domain Name System (DNS) answers queries about names. An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address; an AAAA record maps it to an IPv6 address. In this sample, SBD-DC01.sbd.test resolves to 10.0.10.10. DNS also works on an isolated network without internet access.
AD needs service discovery

Service (SRV) records advertise which servers provide a service. A client uses DNS to discover suitable domain controllers, resolves their hostnames, and contacts a controller for authentication. DNS does not validate the password. A running DC can still be difficult to find if the DNS records or client settings are wrong.
What a zone contains

A DNS zone holds records for a portion of the namespace. With an AD-integrated zone, records are stored in AD DS and replicated to DNS servers within the configured replication scope. Secure dynamic updates restrict which identities may change records. Check the zone scope and update policy on the completed build.
Two roles, two kinds of checks

Installing DNS and installing AD DS provide different services, even when they run on the same server. Query each DNS server for SRV and host records, then check directory replication separately. A correct DNS answer proves neither a successful sign-in nor access to a protected resource.
foundations.takeaway: Discovery sequence: ask DNS for a domain service → resolve the server name → contact a reachable DC → authenticate.
foundations.prompt: If you can reach 10.0.10.10 but cannot discover sbd.test, which DNS records and client settings would you inspect?

foundations.title: Why use two domain controllers?
foundations.summary: Keep identity and DNS services available when one server is unavailable.
blocks: Remove the single-server dependency

With one DC, its outage removes the only live directory service point. With two healthy, reachable controllers, clients can discover a surviving DC for supported operations. This also lets you patch or restart one server while the other continues serving requests. Reconnection may take time; uninterrupted service is not guaranteed.
Both controllers do useful work

Both writable DCs can process normal directory changes and authentication requests. Replication shares directory changes between them. They are not a primary server and an idle spare. Certain operations still depend on a single FSMO role holder, so role placement and recovery need their own plan.
Make the redundancy real

Microsoft recommends at least two virtualized DCs per domain on different virtualization hosts. Two VMs on one host share that host as a failure point. Consider shared storage, power, and network dependencies too. Run DNS on both here, verify zone replication, and configure clients to use both internal DNS addresses.
Availability still needs recovery

Replication can spread an accidental deletion or harmful change to both servers. Keep protected backups and test recovery separately. Two is a starting point for this design, not a universal capacity target: additional sites, users, and recovery needs may require more controllers.
foundations.takeaway: Before relying on DC02, verify replication and DNS, review shared dependencies, and test client discovery during an approved maintenance window.
foundations.prompt: If both controllers run on the same physical host, which outage would still stop both services?
